translations.answer: PHC uses progressive capacity expansion to cover a large reference-motion collection and a dedicated recovery module to return fallen or diverged states to the tracking domain. It reports high coverage on simulated AMASS tests but no physical-robot experiment, so it is a strong scaling and recovery-training baseline rather than a validated perpetual hardware controller.
translations.applicability.assumptions.0: Reference motions have been converted to the simulated humanoid morphology and joint convention used by the paper.
translations.applicability.assumptions.1: Policy capacity, training samples, and failure-state coverage are comparable to the scale reported in the paper.
translations.applicability.controllers.0: PHC progressive motion-tracking and recovery policies
translations.applicability.environments.0: Physics-based tracking over large human-motion collections
translations.applicability.robots.0: The paper's simulated humanoid avatars; these are not direct evidence for a physical robot
translations.confidence_rationale: The paper reports large-scale AMASS tests and recovery ablations, and the official code exposes the key implementation. All evidence is from simulated avatars, however, and cannot establish physical-humanoid deployment performance.
translations.evidence.0.locator: Sections 3-5, Tables 1-3, Figures 2-6, and the appendix
translations.evidence.0.note: Defines progressive multiplicative control, failure-state recovery, and large-scale motion evaluation, including training cost and simulation results.
translations.evidence.0.title: Perpetual Humanoid Control for Real-time Simulated Avatars
translations.terms.0: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU, 惯性测量单元)
translations.title: Has PHC proved that one policy can perpetually track tens of thousands of motions and recover automatically on a physical humanoid robot?
